summary: This randomized, open-label, no-placebo trial (TEAM study) compared lithium, divalproex sodium, and risperidone as initial treatment for 279 antimanic medication-naive children and adolescents (ages 6-15) with DSM-IV bipolar I disorder, manic or mixed phase, over 8 weeks. Risperidone produced significantly higher CGI-BP-IM response rates than lithium (68.5% vs 35.6%, OR 5.0, P<.001) or divalproex sodium (68.5% vs 24.0%, OR 8.3, P<.001), while lithium and divalproex sodium did not differ significantly from each other. Weight gain, BMI increase, and prolactin elevation were significantly greater with risperidone than with either lithium or divalproex sodium, and lithium caused significant increases in thyrotropin levels.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This trial is not lithium-specific: patients received either lithium OR valproate as background mood stabilizer, with olanzapine or placebo added on top. Only ~33-36% of each arm was on lithium (76/229 cotherapy, 41/115 monotherapy); the majority received valproate. Weight-gain adverse-event rates were reported for the full sample AND broken out by mood-stabilizer subgroup (Table 4): lithium subgroup weight gain 21.1% (cotherapy) vs 4.9% (monotherapy), valproate subgroup 28.8% vs 8.2%; full sample 26.2% vs 7.0% (p<.001). summary: This is a French-language narrative review of asenapine (a second-generation antipsychotic) for bipolar I mania/mixed episodes, summarizing efficacy and tolerability data from the ARES and Apollo trial series. Lithium appears only as a background mood stabilizer to which asenapine or placebo was added in the Apollo adjunctive-therapy trials, or as a comparator drug class discussed in passing (e.g., in a meta-analysis of antimanic agents). No original weight, dose, or serum-level data for a lithium treatment arm are reported in this article.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a narrative/non-systematic review of asenapine efficacy and safety in bipolar disorder, not a primary clinical trial of lithium. Lithium is mentioned only (1) as the background mood stabilizer that patients in the 'Apollo' adjunctive-therapy trial (Szegedi et al. 2011/2012) were already stabilized on before randomization to asenapine-vs-placebo add-on (inclusion required serum lithium 0.6-1.2 mmol/L, but no weight or dose data for the lithium arm itself are given — lithium was held constant across both randomized arms, so it is not a distinct study arm for this review's purposes), and (2) as one of several comparator drug classes in a cited meta-analysis of 17 antimanic agents (reference 26/Table showing Hedges' g effect sizes, no weight data). No lithium salt form, dose, serum level achieved, or weight-gain outcome data attributable to a lithium arm are reported anywhere in the text. This paper does not meet the extraction target (a lithium weight-gain clinical trial) and all quantitative fields have been left null/empty per instructions to extract only what is explicitly stated.

summary: This post-hoc analysis of a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial examined whether adding ziprasidone (vs. placebo) to a mood stabilizer (lithium or valproate) affected weight and metabolic parameters during 6 months of maintenance treatment in bipolar I disorder. Body weight change was similar between the ziprasidone+MS and placebo+MS groups at all visits (p>0.05), indicating ziprasidone had a neutral effect on weight when added to lithium or valproate. Because lithium/valproate assignment was not randomized and dose/serum-level data specific to the lithium subgroup were not separately reported, this paper mainly documents that adjunctive ziprasidone does not add to weight-gain risk on a lithium/valproate backbone, rather than characterizing lithium's own dose-response effect on weight.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Both arms received lithium OR valproate as background mood stabilizer (not exclusively lithium), and this allocation was explicitly stated as not randomized; the paper does not separate weight/metabolic results by which mood stabilizer (Li vs VAL) patients received in Phase 2, so lithium-specific dose/serum data for the double-blind phase are not extractable. Phase 1 (open-label) Table 3 does report separate Li+ZIP vs VAL+ZIP body weight change scores (Li+ZIP: baseline 78.6 kg (SD 19.5), change +0.23 kg (95%CI -0.46,0.91), n=225; VAL+ZIP: baseline 83.0 kg (SD 22.6), change +0.54 kg (95%CI -0.09,1.16), n=268) but this is a single-arm (all on active ZIP) stabilization phase with no placebo comparator, so per the extraction scope (primary outcome only, final double-blind timepoint) it was omitted from 'outcomes' — flagging it here as it is the only place lithium-specific weight data with quantitative values appear in this paper. Double-blind Phase 2 body weight change data (Fig. 4D) are presented only as a figure with mean change (kg ± SE) at weeks 4/8/12/16/20/24 and N per arm per timepoint, with no numeric axis values extractable from text, and text states only 'p>0.05 (vs. placebo, all visits)' with no exact p-value; n_analyzed for week 24 (84 ZIP+MS, 53 PBO+MS) taken from Fig. 4D N labels. No lithium salt form, dose in mg, or achieved serum lithium level (mmol/L or mEq/L) is reported anywhere in the paper beyond the protocol target range of 0.6-1.2 mEq/L used for both Phase 1 and Phase 2. Outcome omitted per scope: all secondary/metabolic outcomes (total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, triglycerides, glucose, MetS prevalence/incidence) were excluded from 'outcomes' as instructed, though Table 3 (Phase 1, open-label) contains full quantitative data on these if needed for other purposes.

summary: This randomized withdrawal trial tested whether continuing lurasidone (20-80 mg/d), added to lithium or valproate, prevented recurrence of mood episodes better than switching to placebo (also with lithium or valproate) in 496 stabilized bipolar I patients over 28 weeks. Lurasidone reduced recurrence risk by 29% (HR 0.71, 95% CI 0.49-1.04) but this did not reach statistical significance (p=0.078) on the primary endpoint. Weight and metabolic changes were minimal and similar between groups, though 'weight increased' as an adverse event was reported more often with lurasidone (9.8%) than placebo (5.2%).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This trial is not itself a lithium-monotherapy trial: only ~43% of randomized patients (N=213) were on lithium, the rest on valproate, and the lithium-specific study-design arm above (arm_id 1) actually represents pooled results across BOTH mood stabilizers since the paper does not break down most efficacy/safety/weight data by mood stabilizer subgroup (only serum lithium/valproate concentrations and the mood-stabilizer subgroup HR for the primary time-to-recurrence outcome are reported separately). Per the extraction scope, only the primary outcome (time to recurrence of any mood episode) is extracted in 'outcomes'; per-arm HR breakdown by mood stabilizer (lithium N=213, HR=0.74) is reported in the text but omitted here since it is a subgroup/secondary analysis, not the ITT primary endpoint. All *_quote fields set to null per extraction scope instructions. Weight gain outcome (binary AE 'weight increased': lurasidone 24/246=9.8%, placebo 13/250=5.2%) is documented in adverse_events but not expanded into a full 'outcomes' object because scope restricts 'outcomes' to primary endpoint(s) only. Lithium salt form, dose in mg, and serum level SD were not reported anywhere in the text — only mean trough concentrations by treatment group and phase were given. Sample size per arm for placebo (arm 2) is not explicitly stated as a standalone number for the lithium-only subgroup; only combined N=250 for placebo (all mood stabilizers) is given, so arm_id 2 n_randomized left null since a lithium-only placebo subgroup count is not reported (only overall placebo N=250 for both mood stabilizers combined).

summary: This 8-week single-blind RCT in 83 first-episode psychotic mania patients (aged 15-28) compared chlorpromazine versus olanzapine, both as add-on therapy to lithium (titrated to serum levels 0.5-1.0 mEq/L). Both arms showed marked weight gain (olanzapine 7.7 kg [SE 1.2]; chlorpromazine 5.6 kg [SE 1.2]) with no statistically significant between-group difference in weight gain (P=.217) or BMI change (P=.147); UKU-rated weight gain occurred in 73.7% (olanzapine) and 80.6% (chlorpromazine) of patients, also not significantly different (P=.336).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Lithium salt form not stated anywhere in the paper (dose given only as elemental-agnostic 'lithium' mg/day); set lithium_salt to unknown per L1. No achieved serum lithium level reported, only the protocol target (0.5-1.0 mEq/l, numerically equal to mmol/L). Both study arms received lithium (combination therapy), so both are lithium arms with identical lithium dosing protocol — the antipsychotic (chlorpromazine vs olanzapine) is the randomised variable, not lithium dose, so dose_contrast_within_trial is false and arms were not renumbered by lithium dose (both follow the same lithium titration protocol; arm ordering follows the paper's presentation of chlorpromazine then olanzapine, but arm_id=1 was NOT reassigned to a 'lithium arm' since both arms are lithium arms). Per EXTRACTION SCOPE, only primary outcome (UKU side-effect frequency) extracted in 'outcomes' with per-arm arm_results omitted since a between-group p-value is reported (RR not explicitly given as a numeric ratio in text, only P=.041 for constipation as the sole significant UKU-based difference; no single omnibus primary effect size/RR was reported for overall side-effect frequency so effect_value is null with the constipation p-value as the closest primary-objective effect). Continuous weight-gain (kg) and binary UKU weight-gain adverse event counts are provided in adverse_events per W3, but per EXTRACTION SCOPE only primary outcomes go in 'outcomes' — weight gain was a SECONDARY objective per the paper's own framing (Section 2.3.3), so weight/BMI outcome objects were omitted from 'outcomes' and the raw counts preserved only in adverse_events.per_arm.notable_aes. Sample sizes per arm use total randomized (36 chlorpromazine, 38 olanzapine, sum=74 matches Table 1 'Total sample n=74'); note 83 were randomized but 74 had complete baseline data in Table 1 (9 patients likely withdrew consent before baseline data collection, discussed in Discussion as '9 patients (10.8%) refused to provide informed consent once they recovered').

summary: This single-center, single-blind, randomized crossover pilot trial tested low-dose lithium carbonate (target 300 mg/day, titrated down from an initial 600 mg/day target due to intolerance) versus an off-drug observation year in 23 adults with primary or secondary progressive multiple sclerosis. The primary outcome, percentage brain volume change, did not differ significantly between the lithium and observation years (+0.107 vs -0.355, p=0.346), though secondary patient-reported mood measures (BDI, MSQOL-mental) improved significantly on lithium. Weight gain was reported by 13 of 23 subjects as an adverse event during lithium treatment, with no comparator arm frequency given since the trial used a within-subject crossover design.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per extraction scope instructions, only the primary outcome (PBVC) was extracted in the outcomes array, at the single on-treatment-year vs observation-year comparison; secondary outcomes (EDSS, MSFC, relapses, BDI, MFIS, MSQOL, SDMT, T25FW, 9HPT, PASAT) were omitted per scope. Weight gain data exist only as an adverse-event frequency in Table 3 (13/23 subjects reporting weight gain on lithium during the single-arm crossover exposure year; no separate placebo/comparator arm exists since design is within-subject crossover, so no binary between-arm outcome object could be constructed — captured instead in adverse_events.notable_aes). No serum lithium levels were ever reported as achieved values (protocol target of 0.5-0.8 mmol/L was abandoned early and not tracked to study end); dose_strategy set to clinician_discretion since dosing was fixed by protocol amendment rather than titrated to serum level for most of the trial. This is a crossover design with each subject as own control across two 1-year periods, not a parallel-arm trial, so only one lithium 'arm' is modeled; between_group_effects reflects the paired within-subject comparison (lithium year minus observation year), with the mean_difference and SE calculated from the two reported period means, their p-value (0.346), and back-solving an approximate SE from p-value/t assumptions was NOT done — instead se is left null and ci_95 left null because paper reports p-value only without SD of the paired difference; per output rule 3 this technically should be discarded from pooling, but effect_value and p_value are retained verbatim/calculated for completeness.

summary: This is a secondary moderator/predictor analysis of the TEAM trial, an 8-week randomized comparison of lithium, divalproex, and risperidone in 279 medication-naive children (ages 6-15) with DSM-IV bipolar I disorder in manic or mixed phase. Risperidone produced significantly higher response rates than lithium or divalproex, and this analysis found the treatment advantage of risperidone over lithium/divalproex was moderated by study site, presence of ADHD, and obesity. No continuous or binary weight-gain outcome data are reported in this paper; it focuses on efficacy moderators, not weight/metabolic adverse events.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is a secondary moderator/predictor analysis of the TEAM trial (primary results published separately as Geller et al. 2012, Arch Gen Psychiatry). It reports no weight, BMI, or metabolic adverse-event data whatsoever — obesity at baseline (BMI >=95th percentile) is used only as a baseline moderator variable, not as an outcome. Lithium salt form is not stated anywhere in this paper (only achieved serum level 1.09 mEq/L, SD 0.34, is given), so lithium_salt is 'unknown' per L1. Divalproex final level (113.6, SD 23.0) has no stated units in the text and is not lithium data, so not extracted into lithium fields. Per the narrowed extraction scope, only the primary outcome (responder status) is extracted at its end-of-treatment timepoint; the paper does not report a pooled RR/CI for the overall risperidone-vs-lithium or risperidone-vs-divalproex comparison (only site-stratified RRs in Table 2), so between_group_effects for the overall comparison are set to not_reported. Secondary KMRS outcome, subgroup/moderator RR tables, and site-level breakdowns were omitted per scope instructions. No weight or thyroid/polydipsia data present anywhere in text — this paper likely contributes only to sample characterization, not to the weight-gain meta-analysis itself.

summary: In children (ages 6-15) with bipolar I disorder who were partial or non-responders to an initial anti-manic medication, adding on or switching to risperidone produced higher response rates than adding on or switching to lithium or divalproex over an 8-week open-label trial. Weight gain occurred with all three add-on medications (lithium 1.66±1.97 kg, risperidone 2.8±1.34 kg, divalproex 1.42±1.96 kg), with no statistically significant difference between medications in average weight gain (p=.07), though weight gain adverse-event frequency significantly increased from baseline for both lithium and risperidone add-on groups.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per extraction scope instructions, only the primary efficacy outcome (CGI-BP-IM response) was extracted in 'outcomes'; weight-gain data (continuous kg means/SDs and binary AE-table counts for weight gain, appetite change, thirst, etc. for lithium/risperidone/divalproex add-on groups, plus BMI, BMI z-score, and prolactin) are secondary outcomes and were omitted from 'outcomes' per scope, but weight-gain AE counts are mirrored into adverse_events.per_arm[].notable_aes as instructed by rule W3. Lithium salt form is never specified in the text (only mEq/L blood levels and mg equivalents for divalproex are given), so lithium_salt is 'unknown' per rule L1. No dose in mg/day is reported for lithium at all -- only achieved/target serum levels in mEq/L (treated as numerically equivalent to mmol/L per rule L3). All *_quote fields set to null per extraction scope. Sample sizes per arm for this report (add-on + cross-taper combined) were calculated by summing Table 2/Table 3 group Ns (lithium 30+39=69; divalproex 20+29=49; risperidone 15+21=36), since the paper does not state combined per-medication n_randomized directly for this report population. Response-rate NNT/CI values in between_group_effects are as stated in text but do not cleanly map only to lithium-containing comparisons in all cases (some CIs are for RSP vs DVPX); flagged via effect_quote=null and extra_note fields (non-schema, informational only) since the paper's NNT/CI reporting does not consistently isolate each pairwise comparison's own CI.

summary: This is a pooled dose-response analysis of four randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trials of quetiapine (as monotherapy or combined with lithium/divalproex) for acute mania in bipolar I disorder. Lithium appears only as a co-medication in the combination-therapy arms, with achieved mean serum lithium concentrations of about 0.75-0.76 mEq/L in both quetiapine and placebo groups; no lithium-specific dosing or weight data are reported separately from divalproex or from quetiapine effects. Quetiapine plus Li/DVP produced significantly greater YMRS improvement than placebo plus Li/DVP (55.7% vs 41.6% responders after 3 weeks, p<0.01), with combination-therapy patients gaining an average of 1.97 kg (quetiapine+Li/DVP) versus 0.27 kg (placebo+Li/DVP) by end of treatment, but these weight figures are not broken out by lithium versus divalproex subgroup.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's primary focus is quetiapine dose-response for mania efficacy, not lithium; lithium appears only as an undifferentiated co-medication arm pooled with divalproex ('Li/DVP'), so per-arm lithium-only weight, dose, and demographic data cannot be isolated from this text. Only ~56-60% of combination-therapy patients received lithium specifically (the rest received divalproex); the reported serum concentrations (0.76/0.75 mEq/L) and weight-gain figures (1.97 kg vs 0.27 kg) are for the pooled Li/DVP arms, not lithium alone, so these were extracted as arm-level context but should be treated cautiously as a lithium-attributable estimate. No lithium salt form, dose in mg, or per-arm lithium-only demographic/outcome breakdown is reported anywhere in the text. Per extraction scope, only the primary efficacy outcome (YMRS) was extracted in 'outcomes' with its end-of-treatment between-group result; per-arm means/SDs for YMRS were not given as plain numbers in this text (only percentages/figure references), so arm_results was left empty and only the qualitative p-value threshold was captured for the between-group effect. summary: This is a post hoc NNT/NNH/LHH analysis of two 6-week, placebo-controlled trials of lurasidone for bipolar I depression: one monotherapy trial (20-60 or 80-120 mg/d) and one adjunctive trial (lurasidone 20-120 mg/d added to ongoing lithium or valproate). Lurasidone showed statistically significant efficacy advantages over placebo for response and remission (single-digit NNTs of 5-7) with no clinically meaningful weight or metabolic changes; NNH for weight gain >=7% was non-significant except for monotherapy 20-60 mg/d (NNH 29, 95% CI 15-52318). The paper's focus is benefit-risk quantification rather than the lithium arm itself, which serves only as a stable background therapy in the adjunctive trial with no lithium dose, salt, or serum-level data reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This paper is NOT a lithium-dose trial: lithium (or valproate) is only the background/adjunctive therapy in one of the two source trials, and no lithium dose, salt form, or serum level is reported anywhere in the text — arms 1 and 2 are lurasidone-vs-placebo added to a mixed lithium/valproate background (per Table 1, ~50% on lithium, ~50% on valproate in each arm), so lithium exposure cannot be isolated per-arm and no lithium arm_id is included in derived.lithium_arm_ids. summary: This 16-week double-blind RCT in 39 hospitalized adults with bipolar I disorder (manic phase) and comorbid obsessive-compulsive symptoms compared adjunctive topiramate versus placebo, with both groups also receiving lithium, olanzapine, and clonazepam. YBOCS scores fell in both groups, but significantly more patients on topiramate achieved a >34% reduction in YBOCS score than on placebo (52.9% vs 12.5%, p<0.01); no serious adverse effects occurred, though topiramate was associated with more constipation and decreased libido leading to dropout.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Both arms received lithium as part of a fixed combination (lithium+olanzapine+clonazepam) with topiramate vs placebo as the sole randomized variable, so both study arms are lithium-exposed (lithium_arm_ids includes both) but there is no lithium-only vs non-lithium contrast — flagged as intervention_category 'combination' rather than pure lithium arms. No lithium salt form was stated for either arm (dose given as bare mg, e.g. 'lithium 800', 'lithium: 825') so lithium_salt is 'unknown' per L1; no serum lithium level was reported anywhere in the text. No weight-gain outcome (continuous, BMI, or binary) was reported in this trial; only baseline weight was given in Table 1 (captured in baseline_demographics) — the adverse-event table (Table 2) recorded 'Increased appetite' but not weight gain itself, so reports_weight_outcome is false and no outcome object for weight was created. Per extraction scope instructions, only the primary outcome (YBOCS) is extracted with final timepoint only; the between-group effect is the responder-rate chi-square (p<0.01) rather than a mean difference, since that is what the paper reports as the key result; the raw YBOCS means/SDs are also given as they were reported alongside. summary: This secondary analysis of the Bipolar CHOICE trial randomized 482 adults with bipolar I or II disorder to lithium or quetiapine (both with adjunctive personalized treatment) and followed body weight, BMI, and waist circumference over 24 weeks. Both drugs were associated with modest weight and BMI increases, but quetiapine produced significantly greater increases than lithium (drug x time interaction p=0.003 for weight, p=0.002 for BMI), with waist circumference increasing significantly only in the quetiapine group; baseline binge-eating behavior further amplified these adverse anthropometric effects, especially with quetiapine.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Lithium and quetiapine doses were not reported as fixed mg/day values anywhere in this paper (individually titrated per adjunctive personalized treatment protocol); no serum lithium levels were reported. Per-arm means/SDs for body weight/BMI/waist circumference at 24 weeks appear only in Table 3 broken down by binge-eating subgroup (not as overall per-arm means), so overall arm_results were left null/not_reported per instructions favoring the primary between-group effect (F-stat, p=0.003) rather than fabricating pooled means from subgroup LS-means. Per EXTRACTION SCOPE, only the primary outcome (body weight, the first-listed and most emphasized anthropometric measure) was extracted at the final 24-week timepoint; BMI and waist circumference (secondary outcomes) and the substantial-weight-gain binary AE were omitted from 'outcomes' per instructions, though the SWG counts are mirrored in adverse_events.notable_aes per rule W3. summary: This 6-week, double-blind, placebo-controlled RCT tested adjunctive lurasidone (20-120 mg/day) versus placebo added to background lithium or valproate in 356 outpatients with bipolar I depression. Lurasidone did not significantly separate from placebo on the primary MADRS endpoint at week 6 (LS mean change 11.8 vs 10.4; P=0.176) or the key secondary CGI-BP-S endpoint, despite significant improvement at intermediate weeks. Weight change was minimal and similar between groups (LOCF endpoint change ~0.0 kg placebo+lithium/valproate vs 0.0 kg lurasidone+lithium/valproate), with only a small minority of patients in the lurasidone arm meeting the >=7% weight-gain threshold and none in the placebo arm.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This trial's lithium arm is confounded with valproate: patients were stratified by mood-stabilizer type (lithium OR valproate), and reported lithium dose/serum-level figures (baseline dose 932.6/942.5 mg/d; serum level 0.73-0.82 mEq/L baseline, 0.68-0.79 mEq/L week 6) are pooled across BOTH treatment arms (lurasidone and placebo) rather than being lithium-arm-specific weight results; only 31.8% (lurasidone) and 34.3% (placebo) of patients were actually on lithium (the rest on valproate), so per-protocol lithium-only weight/dose data are not separable from valproate patients in this paper. Lithium salt form was never stated (US/multinational sites, salt likely carbonate by convention but NOT assumed per instructions — set to unknown). Weight outcome (Table 2B, 'Weight, kg' LOCF endpoint change: lurasidone 0.0±2.4 kg, placebo +0.2±1.7 kg) is reported for the OVERALL safety population (both lithium+valproate patients combined), not lithium-arm-specific, so it was not extracted as a continuous outcome object per the narrowed extraction scope (primary outcome only = MADRS); the binary '>=7% weight gain/loss' proportions (3.0% vs 0% each direction) were likewise for the combined lithium/valproate safety population and are mirrored into adverse_events per PROMPT rule W3, with n calculated from 3.0% x N (177 lurasidone, 171 placebo, rounded). Per extraction scope instructions, only the primary MADRS outcome was extracted in the outcomes array; secondary outcomes (CGI-BP-S, QIDS-SR16, HAM-A, Q-LES-Q-SF, SDS, responder/remission rates, lipids, glucose, insulin, prolactin) were omitted. summary: This double-blind, randomized pilot trial compared oxcarbazepine versus carbamazepine as add-on therapy to ongoing lithium maintenance in 52 bipolar I/II outpatients with residual symptoms over 8 weeks. Both drugs improved mood symptoms, with oxcarbazepine significantly more effective than carbamazepine on all five outcome measures; weight gain was reported only as an adverse event, occurring in 11/26 (44.4%) of the carbamazepine group but not explicitly quantified for the oxcarbazepine group, and lithium serum levels were similar and stable across both arms (0.73 vs 0.71 mmol/L) throughout the study. No formal continuous weight or BMI outcome was assessed.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Lithium is the background/index exposure common to both arms (dose and salt form not reported anywhere in the text — only serum levels are given); the randomized comparison is OXC vs CBZ add-on, not different lithium doses, so dose_contrast_within_trial is false. summary: This multicenter double-blind RCT randomized 149 hospitalized patients with unipolar major depression to clomipramine 150 mg/day plus fixed-dose lithium carbonate 750 mg/day (mean serum lithium 0.50 mmol/L) versus clomipramine plus placebo for 6 weeks. The primary endpoint (percentage MADRS reduction by day 11) favored the lithium group but did not reach statistical significance (32.1% vs 27.4%, P=0.07), though several secondary efficacy measures reached significance early in treatment; body weight itself showed no significant between-group difference and no per-arm weight data were reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per protocol, only the primary outcome (percentage MADRS reduction D0-D11) was extracted; secondary efficacy outcomes (mean MADRS/CGI scores, responder/remission rates at D4/D7/D11/D14/D28/D42) were omitted per extraction scope. Weight/body-weight was assessed as a safety parameter and the paper states no significant between-group difference in body weight was found ('No clinical parameter revealed any signiﬁcant difference between the two groups, including systolic and diastolic blood pressure, pulse and body weight'), but no numeric per-arm weight values, weight change, or a discrete adverse-event count for 'weight gain' were reported anywhere in the text or tables — only baseline weight (Table 2) is quantified. Therefore no weight outcome object was created (reports_weight_outcome=false). Lithium salt form and dose were explicitly stated as lithium carbonate 750 mg/day (brand Teralithe, which also maps to carbonate); serum level 0.50 mmol/L (range 0.3-0.8 mmol/L in most patients) was explicitly reported as achieved, not a target — no target range was stated in this trial. dose_contrast_within_trial is false since there is only one lithium dose arm. exposure_stratum set to low_dose_clinical because this is a fixed sub-standard dose (750 mg/day carbonate, ~13 mmol/day) deliberately kept low and targeting/achieving a low serum level (0.5 mmol/L), consistent with the authors' own characterization ('moderately low fixed dose of lithium'). summary: This 52-week double-blind CANMAT trial randomized 159 bipolar I patients who had recently remitted from a manic episode to discontinuation of adjunctive risperidone/olanzapine at entry, at 24 weeks, or continuation for the full 52 weeks, while all patients remained on lithium or valproate. Continuing the antipsychotic for 24 weeks significantly reduced time to any mood episode versus immediate discontinuation (HR 0.53, 95% CI 0.33-0.86), but extending to 52 weeks offered no additional benefit over 24 weeks (HR 1.18, 95% CI 0.71-1.99) and was associated with significantly more weight gain (3.2 kg vs losses of 0.1-0.2 kg in the other groups, p=0.01).

summary: This double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study in 12 healthy male volunteers examined the renal hemodynamic and tubular effects of intravenous urodilatin (a natriuretic peptide) infusion at three doses. A single 300mg oral lithium carbonate dose was administered solely as a pharmacological tracer to measure lithium clearance as an index of proximal tubular sodium handling; lithium was not the study intervention and no weight-gain or psychiatric outcomes were assessed. This paper does not meet eligibility criteria for the lithium weight-gain review.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: INELIGIBLE PAPER: lithium (300mg lithium carbonate tablet, single dose) was administered purely as a renal clearance tracer/marker substance to assess proximal tubular sodium and water handling, not as a therapeutic or supplement intervention. The actual intervention under study is urodilatin (a natriuretic peptide), infused IV at 10/20/40 ng/min/kg vs placebo, in healthy volunteers, for renal hemodynamic outcomes. No weight-gain, metabolic, or psychiatric outcomes relevant to this review are reported (body weight loss during the single study day, ~1-1.2 kg across all groups including placebo, reflects acute fluid/fasting effects, not a lithium exposure effect, and is not attributable to a lithium arm since there is no lithium treatment arm). No lithium dose-response arms, no serum lithium target, no psychiatric diagnosis. Recommend excluding at full-text screening stage.

summary: In this randomized, double-blind trial of 94 patients with bipolar disorder, maintenance lithium carbonate dosed to achieve standard serum levels (0.8-1.0 mmol/L) was compared with lithium dosed to achieve low serum levels (0.4-0.6 mmol/L). The standard-range group had significantly fewer relapses and a lower hazard of relapse (HR 2.6, 95% CI 1.3-5.2, p=0.004 favoring standard range), but side effects including weight gain, tremor, diarrhea, urinary frequency, and metallic taste were more frequent at the higher serum level; weight gain itself was reported only qualitatively (more frequent in the standard-range group) without per-arm counts or percentages.

summary: This 8-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 40 adolescent inpatients with acute bipolar mania tested adjunctive celecoxib (100 mg twice daily) versus placebo, added to background lithium (titrated to serum level 0.8-1.1 mEq/L) and risperidone. Both arms received lithium (not a lithium-vs-non-lithium comparison); this trial contrasts celecoxib vs placebo as an add-on, with lithium+risperidone as background therapy in both arms — lithium_arm_ids includes both arms since both received lithium at similar doses/serum levels (not a dose-contrast design). summary: This 6-week, randomized, double-blind trial compared lithium (target serum level 1.0-1.2 mEq/L) versus quetiapine (target dose 400-600 mg/d) for acute manic or mixed episodes in 109 youths (ages 10-17) with early-course bipolar I disorder. Quetiapine produced a significantly greater reduction in YMRS score than lithium (-13.2 vs -11.0, p<0.001, effect size 0.39) and a higher response rate (72% vs 49%, p=0.012), though remission rates did not differ; quetiapine was also associated with significantly greater weight gain (EMM +3.7 kg vs +1.3 kg, p=0.02) and BMI z-score increase compared with lithium.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Per extraction scope, only the primary outcome (YMRS change) was extracted with its final timepoint and between-group effect; secondary outcomes omitted include treatment response rate, remission rate, CGI-BP-S/I, weight/BMI change (EMM +3.7 kg vs +1.3 kg, p=0.02; BMI z-score percentile shift), laboratory changes (TSH, lipids, WBC, RBC, calcium), QTcF interval change, and predictors of treatment response. Weight/BMI data are reported only as EMM group differences and percentile shifts in the text, not as full per-arm means/SDs or a discrete safety-table AE count with n/N — no binary weight-gain threshold (e.g., ≥7%) was reported, so weight was not extracted as an outcome object under the primary-outcome-only scope of this task, though W1-W4 rules would normally require capturing it as a continuous change_from_baseline outcome (+1.3 kg lithium vs +3.7 kg quetiapine, p=0.02) had secondary outcomes been in scope. summary: This secondary analysis of two pooled 18-month, double-blind, placebo-controlled maintenance trials examined older adults (≥55 years) with Bipolar I disorder randomized to lithium (0.8-1.1 mEq/L, modal dose 750 mg/day), lamotrigine (100-400 mg/day, modal dose 240 mg/day), or placebo. summary: This 6-month, open-label, randomized pilot trial in 49 bipolar outpatients compared continuing an oral atypical antipsychotic versus switching to long-acting injectable risperidone (LAI-ris), with all patients remaining on a mood stabilizer (which could include lithium, valproate, or lamotrigine). extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This trial's arms are defined by antipsychotic strategy (oral AAP continuation vs. switch to LAI-ris), not by lithium exposure — lithium is only one of up to two permitted background mood stabilizers (with valproate/lamotrigine), and the paper never reports what fraction of patients in each arm were on lithium, nor any lithium dose or serum level. Because arms cannot be mapped to distinct lithium exposure levels per the required arm_id=1-is-lithium convention, lithium_arm_ids is left empty and lithium dose/serum fields are null/unknown throughout. Weight is reported only as a narrative safety statement ('no significant changes in weight... within each group' and 'no significant differences between the groups in... weight') with no numeric means, SDs, Ns, or between-group effect estimate given in text or tables — so arm_results is empty and the between-group effect is not_reported. No BMI or binary clinically-significant-weight-gain outcome was reported. This paper is a weak/marginal fit for a lithium-specific weight-gain meta-analysis given the confounded background-therapy design and total absence of quantitative weight data.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: INELIGIBLE PAPER: this is a renal/dopamine physiology study in healthy volunteers using a single lithium test dose (600 mg lithium carbonate, one evening before each study day) purely as a lithium-clearance tracer for proximal tubular function; it is not a therapeutic lithium trial and reports no weight-gain, BMI, or body-composition outcome. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: EXCLUDE FROM META-ANALYSIS: lithium here is a single-dose (400 mg lithium carbonate, given once the evening before each of two clearance study days) pharmacokinetic/renal-physiology tracer used to compute fractional lithium clearance (an index of proximal tubular sodium reabsorption), not a therapeutic or supplement exposure. The body weight change reported (72.2±12.9 to 74.0±12.6 kg, p<0.05) is caused by fludrocortisone (a mineralocorticoid), not by lithium, and reflects sodium/fluid retention during 'escape' physiology, not adiposity or lithium-induced weight gain. summary: This RCT evaluated adjunctive aripiprazole (15-30 mg/day) versus adjunctive placebo added to open-label lithium or valproate monotherapy in 384 bipolar I patients with mania partially nonresponsive to lithium/valproate alone. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is primarily an aripiprazole-adjunctive-therapy trial; lithium is one of two background mood stabilizers (the other being valproate), not the intervention of primary interest for this weight-gain review. Lithium salt form was never specified anywhere in the text, so lithium_salt is 'unknown' for both lithium arms per rule L1. No separate per-arm weight data for the lithium-only subgroup were given numerically (only 'no significant treatment differences in the lithium or valproate subgroups' stated qualitatively) — the only quantitative weight change numbers reported are pooled across lithium+valproate subgroups by treatment arm (aripiprazole +0.55 kg [SD 2.66] vs placebo +0.23 kg [SD 3.51], LOCF), so weight/binary-weight-gain outcomes were extracted at the overall-population level, not lithium-arm-specific, and per instructions the outcomes section only includes the PRIMARY (YMRS efficacy) outcome — weight change is a secondary outcome per this paper's stated hierarchy and was therefore omitted from 'outcomes' per the EXTRACTION SCOPE override (primary outcome only). Per-arm demographics (age, sex, weight, BMI) were reported only for the overall placebo vs aripiprazole groups (Table 1), not broken out by lithium/valproate subgroup, so per-arm demographic fields for arms 1-4 are null; overall-population age/sex were calculated by pooling Table 1's placebo (N=131) and aripiprazole (N=253) rows. Sample size per-arm for lithium/valproate subgroups is by MOOD STABILIZER (Table 1: lithium N=51 placebo/106 aripiprazole; valproate N=80 placebo/147 aripiprazole), not literal randomization arms of a 2-arm trial, but structured this way per instruction to make arm_id=1 the lithium arm. Between-group effect for primary outcome (mean difference -2.6, derived from -13.3 minus -10.7) is an ANCOVA-adjusted estimate as reported by the study (F=9.54, p<0.01), not a simple recalculation from unadjusted per-arm SDs, so no SE could be derived from the two SDs; effect_source set to 'calculated' since the paper did not print a formatted mean-difference value directly. summary: In this North American maintenance trial (Trial 127), 623 patients with bipolar I disorder stabilized on quetiapine plus lithium or divalproex were randomized to continue quetiapine or switch to placebo, while remaining on lithium or divalproex. Continued quetiapine combination therapy significantly reduced the risk of mood-event recurrence versus placebo combination therapy (20.3% vs 52.1%; hazard ratio 0.32, 95% CI 0.24-0.42, p<0.0001). Weight increase, sedation, and hypothyroidism were significantly more common with quetiapine; this extraction focuses on the lithium-cotreatment subset for exposure characterization, as lithium dose/salt/serum-level data specific to the lithium-only subgroup were not separately reported beyond median serum concentration.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This trial's two randomized arms are 'quetiapine + lithium or divalproex' vs 'placebo + lithium or divalproex' — lithium was only one of two permitted co-treatments (divalproex being the other), and the paper does not separately report arm-level lithium salt, dose in mg, or serum levels restricted to the lithium-only subgroup; only overall median lithium serum concentrations (0.74 quetiapine group, 0.71 placebo group) are given across the combined lithium+divalproex randomized population, mixed with divalproex-treated patients. Per EXTRACTION SCOPE instructions, only the primary time-to-event outcome (time to recurrence of any mood event) was extracted; weight-gain and other secondary/AE-table outcomes (weight increase AE counts by arm, mean weight change +0.46 kg quetiapine vs -1.95 kg placebo, BMI change, glucose/lipid changes, hypothyroidism) were omitted from 'outcomes' per scope but weight AE counts were still mirrored into adverse_events.per_arm.notable_aes as instructed by rule W3. Lithium salt form and per-arm mg dose were never stated in the paper (only serum target 0.5-1.2 meq/L), so lithium_salt is 'unknown' for both arms per rule L1. Because this trial does not isolate a pure lithium arm (both randomized groups contain a lithium-or-divalproex mix), dose_contrast_within_trial is false and this paper primarily contributes indirect/mixed lithium exposure data rather than a clean lithium-vs-placebo weight-gain contrast.

summary: This 6-week randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial tested adjunctive midday bright light therapy (7,000-lux white light) versus dim red placebo light in 46 adults with bipolar I/II depression on stable antimanic medication. summary: This post hoc analysis of the CANMAT randomized double-blind trial compared lithium (n=85) and valproate (n=74), each used as monotherapy or with adjunctive olanzapine/risperidone continued for 0, 24, or 52 weeks, in bipolar I disorder maintenance treatment. Weight gain was reported as an adverse event with similar rates in both groups (11% lithium vs 11% valproate), and there were no significant differences between lithium and valproate on the primary efficacy outcome of time to any mood episode (HR 0.99, 95% CI 0.66-1.48, p=0.95).

summary: This narrative review summarizes the Tohen et al. 2005 double-blind RCT comparing lithium monotherapy versus olanzapine monotherapy for relapse prevention in bipolar I disorder over 52 weeks, following open-label co-treatment stabilization. Overall mood episode recurrence did not differ significantly between groups (38.8% lithium vs 30.0% olanzapine, p=0.055), though olanzapine was significantly better at preventing manic and mixed relapses. During the double-blind period, mean weight change was significantly greater with olanzapine than lithium (+1.8kg vs -1.4kg, p<0.001), and significantly more olanzapine patients gained >=7% of baseline weight (29.8% vs 9.8%, p<0.001).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This source is a narrative/review article (Dando & Tohen 2006) summarizing the Tohen et al. 2005 lithium-vs-olanzapine RCT, not the primary trial publication; per-arm continuous weight change (1.8kg vs -1.4kg) and the binary >=7% weight gain proportions (29.8% vs 9.8%) are reported only as aggregate double-blind-phase results without per-arm SDs or exact n at that timepoint, so no separate weight outcome objects were built per the extraction scope (primary outcome only was requested in 'outcomes'; weight data is captured in adverse_events.notable_aes and the summary). Lithium salt form, dose in mg, and achieved/target serum levels beyond the stated 0.6-1.2 mmol/L acute-phase target were not reported in this text. Cholesterol change data (5.4±29.8 mg/dl vs -12.4±29.4 mg/dl) also appears but is a metabolic secondary outcome, out of scope per extraction instructions. Three additional trials (olanzapine vs placebo, olanzapine vs divalproex, olanzapine+mood stabilizer vs mood stabilizer alone) are also described in this paper but contain no lithium arm meeting inclusion criteria as a standalone therapeutic lithium comparison beyond the one extracted (the fourth study's 'mood stabilizer' arm was investigator's choice of lithium OR valproate, not separable into a pure lithium arm), so they were not extracted as separate arms/outcomes.

summary: This 46-week open-label extension study evaluated adjunctive aripiprazole added to lithium or valproate in bipolar I patients who were partial responders to mood-stabiliser monotherapy. Mean weight gain from double-blind endpoint to Week 46 (LOCF) was 2.3 kg (SE 0.6) with aripiprazole+lithium and 2.0 kg (SE 0.4) with aripiprazole+valproate, a small, non-significant difference not formally tested since the study was not powered to compare subgroups. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: Lithium salt form not stated anywhere in the paper (only '250 mg tablets' and dose range in mg/day); left as unknown per L1 rather than assuming carbonate. Serum lithium achieved levels not numerically reported — only percentages of patients within the 0.6-1.0 mmol/L therapeutic range at each visit (67.0%, 81.6%, 69.8%, 73.5%), which do not map to a mean/SD and were left null per L5. Weight change SE values used directly (se field) rather than SD since paper reports mean (SE). Between-group mean difference for weight change (0.3 kg) was calculated from the two arm SEs (sqrt(0.6^2+0.4^2)=0.7211) since no direct between-group comparison/p-value was reported for this outcome (aripiprazole was adjunctive in both arms so this is an ARI+LI vs ARI+VAL comparison, not a lithium vs placebo comparison). Binary 'clinically significant weight gain' outcome (>=7% gain from baseline) omitted per extraction scope narrowing to primary outcome only — the paper reports 23.7% (ARI+LI) vs 28.8% (ARI+VAL) with >=7% gain, and this would normally be a first-class binary outcome per W3, but scope restricts 'outcomes' to primary outcome/timepoint only. Secondary outcomes (YMRS, MADRS, LIFE-RIFT, SF-36, metabolic parameters, EPS scales) omitted per extraction scope. Sample sizes per arm restricted to n_randomized only per scope; n_completed/withdrawals omitted from sample_sizes.per_arm (though present in adverse_events for AE-related counts, which were retained as those are a separate schema section not restricted by scope). No true 'lithium arm vs comparator arm' contrast exists here in the classic sense — both arms received adjunctive aripiprazole; arm 1 is lithium-based combination therapy and arm 2 is the valproate-based combination therapy used as an active comparator per study design, not a placebo/monotherapy lithium contrast.

summary: This one-year double-blind trial compared prophylactic lithium carbonate against maprotiline (a tetracyclic antidepressant) in 39 patients with recurrent affective disorders. The mean Affective Morbidity Index was numerically lower with lithium but not statistically significantly so, though a dichotomized analysis (no morbidity vs some morbidity) found lithium significantly superior to maprotiline overall (p<0.02) and in unipolar patients specifically (p<0.05). Weight-related findings were incidental: a highly significant negative correlation (r=-0.97, p<0.001) was found between plasma maprotiline concentration and body weight, with no quantitative weight-gain data reported for the lithium arm.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper does not report quantitative weight data for the lithium arm at all — weight was recorded on the affective disorders chart per methods, but no lithium-arm weight/BMI values or weight-gain adverse-event counts appear in text or tables. No continuous body weight (kg) outcome was reported; the paper instead reports a Hamilton Depression Scale 'weight loss' factor score, finding lithium non-responders had significantly higher (worse) baseline weight-loss and sleep-disturbance scores than responders, and that T3 responders had higher weight-loss factor scores than lithium responders (p<0.05). No true body-weight-gain data suitable for this meta-analysis were reported.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This paper does not report actual body weight, BMI, or weight-gain adverse-event data for lithium; it only reports a Hamilton Depression Scale 'weight loss' factor subscore (an item cluster measuring appetite/weight loss as a depressive symptom, NOT weight gain as a lithium side effect), used here as a predictor of antidepressant-augmentation response. Given this, the outcome extracted is not usable for the weight-gain meta-analysis and reports_weight_outcome is set to false. Lithium dose is a fixed range (900-1200 mg/day) with no salt form stated (set to unknown per rules) and no per-arm breakdown by exact dose. Achieved serum lithium level (mean 0.68 mmol/L, range 0.56-0.93) was reported for the lithium group as a whole with no difference between responders/non-responders, but no SD was given. OCR artifacts in the source text (e.g. 'HRSD', garbled table formatting) made some table values unparseable/ambiguous; Tables 2-4 report F/p values for response and treatment effects on Hamilton factor scores rather than per-arm weight data usable for pooling. Secondary outcomes and full HRSD/thyroid tables omitted per extraction scope (primary-outcome-only instructions), and no genuine 'primary outcome' for weight gain exists in this paper.

summary: This double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled crossover study tested 4 weeks of metformin (850 mg twice daily) versus placebo in nonobese, insulin-resistant, essential hypertensive patients. Metformin improved insulin-mediated glucose disposal and increased urinary cation excretion without changing blood pressure or body mass index, which was identical after both treatments (24.5 ± 2.2 kg/m2). Lithium was used only as a single-dose renal clearance tracer (16.2 mmol lithium carbonate given orally the evening before each metabolic study day), not as a therapeutic agent, so this paper is not a true lithium weight-gain trial.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a lithium therapeutic trial. Lithium carbonate (16.2 mmol single oral dose) was administered only as a renal clearance tracer to measure cation excretion/heteroexchange at the end of each crossover period — it was given identically during BOTH the metformin and placebo periods, so there is no lithium-vs-control arm contrast and no lithium dosing regimen to extract per the schema's arm structure. The actual randomized intervention is metformin vs placebo for insulin resistance/hypertension. The only weight-related outcome is BMI (identical 24.5±2.2 kg/m2 after both placebo and metformin), reported as a single value each with no separate n or SD breakdown by arm beyond what's quoted; no per-arm sample sizes (n randomized) are stated anywhere in the text. Given the review's scope is lithium weight-gain trials, this paper likely should have been screened out at full-text eligibility — flagging this concern. No adverse event weight data, no serum lithium level, no lithium dose-response data of any kind relevant to this meta-analysis.

Per extraction scope instructions, only the primary/final timepoint's between-group effect would normally be extracted, but this is a single-arm pre/during/post design with no between-group comparison, so within_group_change was used instead per rule 2; all three timepoints were kept because none is a true 'intermediate' timepoint being skipped — each is a distinct clinically meaningful state (before/during/after) rather than serial follow-ups within one treatment period. summary: This cross-sectional study of 63 current lithium users in Canada examined whether environmental temperature affects serum lithium levels, renal parameters, and the lithium dose-to-serum-level ratio. No body weight outcome data were reported; this paper is not usable for weight-gain meta-analysis but provides baseline dose/serum-level data.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a pharmacokinetic study, not a weight-gain trial; BMI change (0.83-3.73 kg/m2 increase by end of pregnancy) is reported only as a range across 3 participants in the Results narrative with no per-patient breakdown, no baseline BMI mean/SD, and no SD/CI for the change itself — so within_group_change.change_mean/change_sd are null and only the range is captured in change_ci_95_low/high (a repurposing, not a true CI). summary: This cross-sectional biocultural study compared self-reported and interview-elicited side effects of chronic lithium therapy among 45 lithium-monotherapy and 25 lithium-plus-neuroleptic/antidepressant ('polypharmacy') Hong Kong Chinese psychiatric outpatients versus 70 matched healthy controls. Weight gain was reported by 24% of lithium-only patients versus 16% of controls (not significantly different), while the polypharmacy group had significantly more weight gain (64%) and a significantly higher mean BMI (24.3 kg/m2) than both the lithium-only (22.2 kg/m2) and control (21.2 kg/m2) groups (Kruskal-Wallis P<0.005), suggesting lithium monotherapy alone did not induce excessive weight gain in this population but polypharmacy did.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's primary focus is transcultural phenomenology of lithium side effects, not weight per se, but it reports quantitative weight-related data (Table I item 19 'weight gain' frequency/mean score, and mean BMI per group) for three groups: lithium-only (N=45), polypharmacy (N=25, excluded from arms per scope since it is not a pure lithium exposure), and healthy control (N=70). Per extraction scope, only primary outcomes at final timepoint were extracted (this is a single cross-sectional timepoint, no baseline/follow-up structure). Dose and serum level values given are means (S.D., range) for the whole lithium-treated group (N=45 lithium-only; overall N=70 including polypharmacy for dose/level stats), not separated further; lithium salt form is not stated in text (Hong Kong prescribing overwhelmingly uses carbonate, hence 'inferred_from_brand' as a weak inference — treat with caution). Weight-gain and excessive-urine/dry-mouth/etc. sample counts in adverse_events.notable_aes were back-calculated from the percentages in Table I (mean score/percent format) and rounded to nearest integer; treated as calculated. Polypharmacy arm (N=25) was omitted from formal 'arms' per this schema's arm_id=1 (intervention) / arm_id=2 (comparator) structure, since it represents a distinct combination-therapy group rather than the lithium/control contrast; its weight gain (64%) and BMI (24.3) data are described only in the summary/extractor notes, not as a full arm object, to avoid conflating polytherapy with lithium monotherapy exposure. summary: This is a Swedish observational cohort of 37 outpatients with major affective disorder maintained on long-term lithium, re-examined at baseline (1980) and 7 years later (1987) for abnormal involuntary movements and related clinical/biochemical variables. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is only marginally relevant to a lithium-specific weight-gain review: it is a mixed case series of 100 patients receiving add-on topiramate for weight gain caused by antipsychotics, lithium, OR valproate, with only 6.1% (Table 1) on lithium as their mood stabilizer, and 90% of the lithium/valproate subgroup also on a concomitant antipsychotic. summary: This post-hoc analysis of the EMBLEM observational study compared 2-year outcomes of olanzapine monotherapy (n=313) versus olanzapine combination therapy (n=763, including 20.3% combined with lithium) in bipolar patients following an acute manic/mixed episode. During the maintenance phase, the monotherapy group had significantly greater mean weight gain (1.4 kg vs. 0.4 kg, p=0.024) and a much higher proportion with ≥7% weight gain (54.8% vs. 19.4%, p<0.001), while the combination group had more tremor, sexual dysfunction, akathisia, and polyuria/nocturia. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This paper is not itself a lithium-specific study — it is an observational bipolar disorder study of olanzapine monotherapy vs. combination therapy, where lithium is only one of several possible add-on agents in the combination arm (20.3% of combination patients took lithium; exact lithium dose, salt form, and serum levels for these patients are not reported anywhere in the text). No lithium-specific arm can be isolated from the reported data, so lithium_arm_ids is empty and all lithium dose/serum fields are null/unknown/not_applicable. Weight outcomes were extracted as the two PRIMARY forms per W1/W3 (continuous change-in-kg and binary ≥7% threshold); the risk_ratio between-group effect for the binary outcome could not be back-calculated with a valid CI from the given p-value alone, so effect_value/CI were left null (only p_value populated) per rule 5's requirement to avoid fabricating precision. SD used for combination arm 95%CI was not computable without raw group SDs beyond what's reported; se for the continuous mean_difference was calculated as sqrt(5.5^2/313 + 7.4^2/763). Numerous other secondary outcomes (relapse, remission, recovery, improvement HRs; other AEs; baseline table 1/2/3 details) were omitted per the EXTRACTION SCOPE instruction to include only primary outcome(s).

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a psychometric validation/reliability study of the UKU-SERS-Pat side-effects scale in a mixed bipolar cohort, not a lithium dose-response or weight-gain outcome study. No lithium dose, salt form, or serum level is reported anywhere in the text (only that 55/93 patients, 59.1%, were 'treated with lithium' as part of polypharmacy). No arms are defined by exposure since this is not a comparative treatment study — all 93 patients form one cross-sectional cohort with heterogeneous, unspecified medication regimens. 'Weight gain' appears only as one item on the side-effects checklist, reported as a prevalence percentage (patient-rated 43.0% vs clinician-rated 35.5%) with a Spearman correlation (r=0.79) and a mean severity-difference score (0.10, SD 0.47) between patient and clinician ratings — these are item-level severity/frequency scores on the UKU scale, not kg, %, or BMI weight-change data, and are not per-lithium-arm. 'Weight loss' is reported similarly (19.4% vs 11.8%). Because there is no lithium-specific arm, no dose/serum data, and no quantitative weight metric usable for meta-analysis, no outcomes array entries were extracted; this paper should likely be excluded from the quantitative synthesis at the screening stage.

summary: This is a narrative review by a UK consultant psychiatrist on the socio-economic and health effects of lithium clinic treatment for manic-depressive illness, covering employment, relationships, suicide, renal and thyroid function, and weight gain. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a narrative/review article, not a primary quantitative trial; most content (employment, relationships, suicide, renal/thyroid sections) is anecdotal or references other cited studies rather than reporting the author's own numeric data, so only the weight/BMI matched comparison (referencing Armond AD, Lithium and weight gain, Br J Psychia 1996;169:251-252, ref 14) was extracted as the primary outcome per instructions. No SD, CI, or exact p-value given for the BMI comparison — only 'in paired t-tests weight gain was not significant' is stated, so p_value is left null and between-group effect_value (0.2 BMI units) was calculated as a simple difference of reported means with no available uncertainty (se/CI could not be computed — no SDs reported). summary: This retrospective chart review examined 14 adolescents with TCA-resistant nonbipolar major depression who had lithium added to their ongoing tricyclic antidepressant treatment. summary: This cross-sectional/prospective study assessed glucose tolerance (oGTT) and body weight in 49 outpatients on long-term lithium maintenance therapy (mean 6.4 years) compared to large German reference populations. The lithium-treated patients showed significantly more pathological oGTT curves and significantly more overweight/obesity than expected from the general population (p<0.01 for weight distribution), though the authors attribute this mainly to weight gain and patient vulnerability rather than a direct pharmacological effect of lithium.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper's primary focus is glucose tolerance, not weight; body weight/BMI data appear only as a categorical distribution (Table III) compared against an expected population distribution (n=1950 reference sample), with no per-patient mean/SD kg or BMI values given, so the weight outcome was extracted as a binary/categorical distribution (proportion overweight/obese: 33/49 = 67.3% observed vs ~32.1% expected) rather than continuous kg or BMI change — there is no baseline/pre-lithium weight measurement (this is a cross-sectional assessment during ongoing treatment, not pre-post). No numeric lithium dose (mg/day) or salt form is given anywhere in the text; only serum lithium concentrations are reported, and only for pathological (0.77 ± 0.25 mEq/1) vs normal (0.66 ± 0.15 mEq/1) oGTT subgroups (not as an overall arm value), so per the schema's arm-level serum_lithium fields these were left null rather than reported as a subgroup comparison — this subgroup contrast (Li plasma level pathological vs normal oGTT, both mEq/L numerically = mmol/L) is present in the results text but excluded here per the narrowed extraction scope (primary outcome only, no secondary oGTT/insulin outcomes). Per the extraction-scope instructions, all *_quote fields are set to null and only the primary (weight) outcome is extracted; the paper's true primary outcome (glucose tolerance/oGTT) was omitted as instructed to focus on weight-related data for this review.

It is NOT a study of lithium as a drug, supplement, or environmental exposure — 'lithium' here refers only to a laboratory reagent used to measure sodium transport kinetics in vitro, and no participant received or was exposed to lithium. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: IRRELEVANT PAPER — NOT A LITHIUM WEIGHT-GAIN STUDY. This is a laboratory/epidemiological study of sodium-lithium countertransport (Na-Li CT), an in-vitro erythrocyte ion-transport assay where lithium chloride is used as a reagent in a cell-washing/incubation protocol to measure sodium efflux kinetics, correlated with body mass index, blood pressure, uric acid, glucose, alcohol intake, etc. No participant ingested or was exposed to lithium as a treatment, supplement, or environmental/drinking-water source. There is no lithium dose, serum lithium level (achieved or target), or weight-gain outcome data of the kind this review requires. The paper's own BMI data (Table 1) reflect the general population sample's baseline anthropometrics, not a lithium-exposure effect, and are not extracted as an outcome. This paper should likely be excluded from the review during screening; flagging for review rather than fabricating any lithium/weight fields.

Serum lithium levels were not measured/reported — only current daily dose in mg and RDIC-derived 'assumed daily dosage' (a chronicity-weighted exposure index, not a true dose) were used. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper does not report any weight, BMI, or weight-gain outcome — its focus is paraoxonase-1 activity and lipid profile (cholesterol, LDL, HDL, ApoA1, ApoB, Lp(a)) in bipolar I patients vs controls. It is included here only because it reports a treatment-subgroup comparison in which lithium-treated patients (n=5) had the lowest paraoxonase activity. No lithium salt form, dose, or serum lithium level is reported anywhere in the text. BMI is reported only as a group-level demographic/stratification variable (Table 1 and Table 3), not as an outcome of lithium treatment, so it was not extracted as an outcome. The between-group effect (lithium vs carbamazepine, 73±45 vs 175±114) was calculated as a mean difference with SE = sqrt(45^2/5 + 114^2/8) ≈ 44.9; footnote indicates 'A vs B: P<0.05' for this comparison. Given the extremely small n=5 lithium subgroup and complete absence of weight/dose data, this paper contributes essentially nothing to the weight-gain meta-analysis.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a retrospective chart-review study of reasons for lithium DISCONTINUATION, not a clinical trial measuring weight change directly. A parallel breakdown by diagnosis type (BPAD1/SZD vs BPAD2/Other) and by agent (doctor vs patient) exists in Table 2 for weight gain (19/253, 22/308, 12/225, 29/334 respectively) but was omitted per extraction scope (primary outcome only, no subgroups). summary: This is a large German-speaking-country pharmacovigilance surveillance study (AMSP, 1993-2016) of 462,661 psychiatric inpatients comparing rates of severe adverse drug reactions (ADRs) between older (≥65 years, n=99,099) and younger (<65 years, n=363,562) patients across all psychotropic drug classes, including lithium. Weight gain (and changes in body weight generally) as a severe ADR was reported far less frequently in older patients across the whole cohort (RR 0.07, 95% CI 0.04-0.14 for weight gain specifically), a highly significant difference, though this outcome was not lithium-specific and reflects spontaneously reported ADR case counts rather than measured weight change. Lithium itself was associated with a significantly higher overall ADR risk in older versus younger patients (RR 1.74, 95% CI 1.52-2.00), and older patients on lithium received lower median doses (450 mg/d vs 900 mg/d) with higher doses in ADR cases within the ≥65 group (737.5 mg/d) than in the overall exposed ≥65 group.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is NOT a lithium-specific weight-gain study; it is a pharmacovigilance analysis of ADRs across all psychotropic drug classes stratified by age, with lithium as one of many drug classes examined and 'weight gain'/'changes in body weight' reported only as an all-psychotropic-drug (not lithium-specific) severe-ADR count, per Table 3. No lithium-specific weight gain data are given anywhere in the text (lithium's own ADR analysis in Fig 3/Table 5/suppl. Table 5 covers overall ADR risk, not weight specifically). Per extraction scope instructions, all *_quote fields were set to null. Lithium salt was inferred as 'carbonate' because Table 4 explicitly lists the drug as 'Lithium carbonate' with dose ranges — this is verbatim, not inferred. Because weight gain figures (10/99,099 and 493/363,562 events) are ADR case counts among ALL psychotropic-drug-exposed patients (not lithium-exposed patients specifically), this outcome is only weakly relevant to the lithium weight-gain review and should be treated with caution — it does not isolate lithium's contribution to weight gain. No serum lithium levels, target ranges, or lithium-specific weight/BMI data are reported anywhere in this paper. Secondary outcomes (delirium, EPS, hyponatremia, falls, etc.) were omitted per extraction scope rules restricting outcomes to primary weight-related outcome only.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a psychiatric case report of anti-NMDAR encephalitis, not a lithium weight-gain study. Lithium was given briefly during initial (incorrect) treatment for presumed bipolar mania, produced no clinical benefit, and was tapered off before tumor surgery; no lithium dose, salt form, or serum level was ever reported. The only weight datum (100kg->90kg) is a weight LOSS at 7-month follow-up explicitly attributed by the patient to lingering effects of corticosteroid (prednisolone/methylprednisolone) treatment for the autoimmune encephalitis, not to lithium, and lithium exposure had ended months earlier. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a comparative observational cohort (lithium vs valproate/olanzapine/quetiapine), not a placebo/no-treatment comparison; lithium is the reference arm and effect estimates for the other three drugs are relative to lithium. Dosage and serum lithium level data were explicitly not captured by the study ('inability to examine dosage effects'), so all lithium dose/serum fields are null. Per scope instructions, only the primary weight-gain outcome (>15% weight gain, PS-adjusted HR) is extracted at its single endpoint timepoint; >7% weight gain, CKD, thyroid, hypercalcemia, T2DM, CVD, hypertension, and hepatotoxicity outcomes were omitted as secondary per extraction scope, though their AE counts are preserved in adverse_events.per_arm for completeness. Non-lithium arms are not lithium-relevant per se but are needed as the comparator for the primary weight outcome. Treatment duration weeks calculated from stated median 1.48 years (1.48*52.14≈77.1 weeks) — set to calculated source.

summary: This was a double-blind, uncontrolled, dose-ranging trial of intravenous Iodine-Lithium-alpha-Dextrin (Armenicum), an experimental antimicrobial/immunomodulatory infusion containing a trace amount of lithium chloride (0.004 g per 20 mL dose), given to 56 antiretroviral-naive HIV-infected patients across three dose groups (0.1, 0.2, 0.3 ml/kg) over 48 weeks. The drug reduced viral load and immune activation markers in symptomatic/AIDS patients and improved quality of life, with body weight (reported only as a pooled overall mean, not per-arm) rising from a baseline of ~65-73 kg to 69.5 ± 4.4 kg at week 48 with no statistical test reported. This paper is not informative for lithium-induced weight gain given the negligible lithium content and near-total absence of lithium dose/serum data.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is almost certainly a false-positive hit for the lithium weight-gain review. IL-alpha-D (Armenicum) is a multi-component iodine/polyvinyl-alcohol/dextrin antimicrobial infusion whose lithium chloride content is trivial (0.004 g = 4 mg lithium chloride per 20 mL dose, i.e. ~0.66 mg elemental lithium at 0.1-0.3 ml/kg, roughly 3-10 mg total per infusion) — far below any pharmacologic/psychiatric lithium exposure, and lithium is not the intended active agent (iodine is). No lithium dose-per-day, serum lithium, or dose-response-by-lithium data are reported; the 3 'dose' arms refer to the whole IL-alpha-D formulation volume, not lithium dose per se, so dose_contrast_within_trial is set to false despite 3 nominal arms. Body weight is reported only as a single pooled value across all 56 patients/doses (not broken out per arm), given as 68.2±2.8 kg (wk12), 70.3±3.2 kg (wk24), 72.4±3.7 kg (wk36), 69.5±4.4 kg (wk48); only the final timepoint was extracted per protocol and could not be assigned to a specific dose arm, so it is reported as a single arm_results entry without an arm_id link to a specific dose group (approximated as arm_id 1, but this is a pooled figure, not arm-1-specific — flagging for reviewer). No baseline (week 0) weight was given for the pooled group (only per-arm baseline weights in Table 1). No between-group statistical comparison of weight was reported. lithium_salt set to 'chloride' per the verbatim formulation ('lithium chloride - 0.004 g') though this is not an oral lithium salt for psychiatric use. Given the exposure stratum, this maps most closely to 'drinking_water' (trace/incidental environmental-level lithium exposure) rather than any clinical dosing stratum, though the O1 ecological-water framework does not perfectly fit an IV infusion context either. Recommend excluding this paper from the lithium weight-gain meta-analysis given lack of relevance to therapeutic lithium exposure.

summary: This naturalistic, retrospective single-arm study followed 30 bipolar adolescents (mean age 14.2 years) treated with lithium carbonate (mean dose ~843-858 mg/day, achieving mean serum levels of 0.69-0.70 mEq/L) for 8 months. Lithium was associated with significant clinical improvement (CGI-S, C-GAS) and was generally well tolerated; in a subset with BMI data, mean BMI rose non-significantly from 18.7 (SD 3.4) at baseline to 19.7 (SD 3) at 8 months, with no patients discontinuing lithium due to excessive weight gain.

summary: This single-center cross-sectional study measured steady-state serum lithium concentrations (after 1.0 g/day oral lithium carbonate for 1 week) in 186 Chinese Han patients with bipolar disorder and examined physiological correlates. Serum lithium was positively associated with creatinine, Mg2+, and neutrophil percentage, and negatively associated with HDL, apolipoprotein A1, and Na+ on Pearson correlation, with Na+ and neutrophil percentage remaining significant in multivariate regression. The study does not report body weight, BMI change, or any weight-gain outcome, so it contributes only dose/serum-level exposure data (not weight outcome data) to this review.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper reports no weight, BMI, or metabolic outcome data anywhere in the text, tables, or figures — it is a study of physiological (renal/lipid/electrolyte/hematologic) correlates of serum lithium concentration only. baseline_demographics BMI (24.21 ± 4.41 kg/m2, Table 1) is reported as a covariate, not an outcome, so it is captured only in baseline_demographics. No outcomes array entries were created per the EXTRACTION SCOPE (primary outcomes only) since no weight/metabolic primary outcome exists in this paper. Dose of lithium carbonate (1.0 g/d = 1000 mg/day) is a fixed protocol dose for achieving steady state, not a titrated treatment dose; percent female not reported anywhere in text or Table 1 (only age/BMI/labs given).

summary: This ecological study correlated county-level trace lithium concentrations in Texas public drinking water (median 0.04 mg/L) with changes in age-adjusted Alzheimer's disease mortality between 2000-2006 and 2009-2015 across up to 234 counties. Higher trace lithium was significantly associated with smaller increases in AD mortality (r = -0.20, p = 0.01), and lithium levels were also negatively correlated with county-level obesity (p = 0.05) and type 2 diabetes prevalence (p < 0.0001), though these are population-level associations, not individual lithium dosing or individual weight change data.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: MD was garbled, used PDF text. This is a county-level ecological/correlational study (Texas drinking water lithium vs. AD mortality), not an individual-level treatment study. No individual dose, serum level, or per-person weight/BMI data are reported. Obesity and type 2 diabetes prevalence are county-level aggregate percentages correlated with log-transformed lithium concentration (Table 3, Fig. 3), not weight-change outcomes in lithium-exposed individuals, so no continuous or binary weight-gain outcome could be extracted per the schema; 'reports_weight_outcome' is set true only because obesity prevalence (a related metabolic measure) is reported, but weight_reported_as is 'none' since no actual body-weight/BMI change data exist. Exact r/p values for lithium-obesity and lithium-diabetes correlations are stated in text (obesity p=0.05, diabetes p<0.0001) but r values for these specific correlations are only shown in Fig. 3, not stated numerically in text. Per-arm sample sizes (n counties above/below median) are not explicitly reported. Per instructions, all *_quote fields are set to null.

summary: This ecological study compared 73 rural and 82 Texas counties, finding rural counties had significantly lower tap water lithium concentrations (33.4 vs 63.3 ug/L) and higher obesity prevalence (30.2% vs 29.1%) and diabetes prevalence (11.0% vs 9.7%) than urban counties. summary: This is an 18-year single-patient case report of a boy with very-early-onset (age 11) bipolar affective disorder treated sequentially with lithium carbonate (alone and combined with valproate), valproate alone, and adjunctive antidepressants. Lithium (up to 1000 mg/day, achieved serum levels 0.57-0.65 mmol/L) was reported as effective and safe over the long term, with only minor side effects (finger tremor) and no quantitative weight or metabolic data reported; when lithium was discontinued in favor of valproate alone, depressive symptoms recurred and resolved again after lithium was reinstated.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a single-patient longitudinal case report (18 years of observation), not a group study — no quantitative weight, BMI, or metabolic outcome data are reported anywhere in the text for the lithium-treated periods; the only weight-related figure in the whole paper is an ~8 kg weight gain attributed to OLANZAPINE (not lithium) during an earlier manic episode, which is excluded from lithium arms per scope. No 'outcomes' array entries were created because the primary outcome for this review (weight) has zero quantitative data. Per protocol instructions, all *_quote fields were set to null. Lithium dose/serum data were extracted across five sequential treatment phases (dose_contrast_within_trial=true) since the same patient received different lithium regimens over time; narrative citations of OTHER studies (Masi et al. 2018, Strober et al. 1990, Findling et al. 2005, Hafeman et al. 2019) within the discussion were not extracted as this paper's own data — they are secondary literature review content, not primary data from this case.

extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper is not a weight-gain study and reports no weight, BMI, or metabolic-syndrome-component outcomes broken out by lithium exposure. It is a retrospective cognitive-impairment risk-factor analysis in which 'Lithium salt (mg)' cumulative dose over 18 months is reported only as an overall/diagnosis-subgroup mean ± SD (e.g., All: 509,457.8 ± 466,414.9 mg; BP: 512,580.4 ± 40,008.5; MDD: 200,544.4 ± 41,526.5; SCH: 188,940.0 ± 21,456.1, Table 2) with no lithium salt form specified, no serum lithium levels, and no defined lithium-only treatment arm (patients received polypharmacy with unspecified proportions on lithium vs. other agents). No arms, sample sizes per arm, or outcomes could be extracted per the lithium-dose or weight-outcome schema since there is no discrete lithium-exposed group with weight data — only a population-wide cumulative-dose covariate in a logistic regression for cognitive impairment. summary: This retrospective South Carolina Medicaid claims cohort study (1996-2005) compared 3,657 children/adolescents prescribed an antimanic medication (lithium 7.9%, carbamazepine 26.2%, valproic acid derivatives 83.0%, often with coprescribed antipsychotics/antidepressants/psychostimulants) to 4,500 untreated Medicaid controls. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This paper does NOT report lithium-specific dose, salt form, or serum level data (explicitly stated as a limitation: 'dosage information in the pharmacy file was not a reliable indicator... so this clinical information was omitted from the presentation'). summary: This case report describes a single breastfeeding infant whose mother was maintained on lithium carbonate 400 mg twice daily for bipolar disorder. The infant initially showed poor weight gain (10 g over 10 days) requiring temporary formula supplementation, but gained weight adequately thereafter with exclusive breastfeeding, while infant serum lithium levels remained minimal (<0.2 mmol/L) and renal/thyroid function stayed normal throughout follow-up to 5.5 months. extraction_metadata.extractor_notes: This is a maternal-lithium/breastfeeding infant case report, not a study of a lithium-treated patient's own weight gain — the 'exposure' arm here is the breastfed infant, and the weight outcome (poor initial weight gain, resolved after temporary supplementation) is plausibly attributable to feeding/lactation issues rather than a direct pharmacologic effect of the trace lithium the infant received via breast milk (infant serum lithium <0.2 mmol/L throughout, per Table 1). Maternal dose was 400 mg/12h = 800 mg/day lithium carbonate (calculated by doubling the stated per-dose amount); brand Plenur® confirmed carbonate salt. No maternal serum lithium level was reported, only infant levels (all <0.2 mmol/L, a detection floor rather than a precise value, so left null/not extracted as a mean). Given the single N=1 design and that the weight outcome is in the infant (not the lithium-exposed adult), this paper contributes essentially no usable quantitative data to a lithium-weight-gain meta-analysis in treated patients; flagging for likely exclusion or narrative-only use.
